sections.overview: The Common Raven is a large member of the crow family, occupying much of the Northern Hemisphere. Its success comes from a flexible way of life: it can hunt, scavenge, eat plant matter, and exploit food made available by people.
sections.identification: An adult measures about 58–69 cm from bill to tail, with a wingspan of roughly 120–150 cm and a mass of about 0.7–1.6 kg; body dimensions vary geographically. It is entirely black, with a heavy bill, thick neck, shaggy throat feathers, and a long, wedge-shaped tail. In comparison, a Carrion Crow is smaller and has a squarer tail, a slimmer bill, and a less shaggy throat; size and silhouette together are more useful than colour, which is black in both. Young ravens look browner and duller than adults. The raven's broad, pointed wings support slow flaps, soaring, and agile rolls or steep dives. Its deep, rough croak carries far, and the species also makes a varied set of softer calls; vocal sounds serve contact, alarm, and territorial contexts.
sections.habitat: Across its range, the raven uses tundra, mountains, coasts, forests, open country, farmland, and some settlements. It needs suitable ledges, trees, or structures for nesting and enough food nearby; consequently, local abundance depends on landscape and resources rather than a single preferred habitat.
sections.diet: The raven is an opportunistic omnivore. It takes carrion, small mammals, birds and their eggs or nestlings, fish, insects and other invertebrates, as well as grains, fruit, buds, and human food waste. Small prey may be swallowed whole, while hairs, feathers, bones, and other poorly digested remains can be brought back up in compact pellets. It hides surplus food in caches, particularly when a large carcass or other temporary bounty is available, and may move or conceal a cache when competitors are nearby.
sections.behavior: Breeding adults usually live as territorial pairs and may remain paired year-round; they defend the nest area and key food patches. Outside these territories, young birds and nonbreeders often gather, and several ravens may converge on a carcass, rubbish tip, or seabird colony. Its characteristic call is a harsh, resonant croak; during courtship, ravens perform tumbling aerial displays. In captive studies, ravens have adjusted cache placement after observing competitors. In one controlled experiment, they guarded caches in response to a rival’s sounds when a peephole allowed that bird to see the caching area; this suggests sensitivity to visual access, without establishing human-like thought.
sections.reproduction: A pair generally establishes and defends a territory before nesting. It builds a bulky stick platform in a tree, on a cliff, or on a human-made structure, then lines the cup with softer material. The female usually incubates a clutch of three to seven eggs for about 20–25 days, while the male often brings food. Chicks hatch helpless, with closed eyes and sparse down; both parents feed them. They leave the nest after roughly four to seven weeks, though fledging does not mean immediate independence. Ravens commonly raise one brood in a year, and young birds may not breed until two to four years old.
sections.ecology: At carcasses, ravens feed alongside other scavengers; in some seabird colonies, groups take eggs and chicks, so their effects on prey are strongly local. The species is thus both a consumer of carrion and a predator whose impact can matter for vulnerable nesting birds.
sections.conservation: The 2021 European Red List assessment classified the breeding population as Least Concern and increasing; this regional assessment is not a guarantee that every local population is secure. In Britain, raven numbers fell historically and the range contracted westward; as persecution eased from the mid-twentieth century, populations recovered and expanded again. The return has renewed conflicts with livestock interests and conservation managers where ravens take vulnerable young or eggs. The British Trust for Ornithology reports licensed control in Scotland and concern that illegal killing may still affect some local populations.
